title: Who wrote this codebase, and what did they touch?
summary: Answer the questions you get on day one at a new job: who are the main contributors, which files change most, and who should review this pull request.
mental_model: Every 'who owns this' question is a `git log` with a different grouping. shortlog groups by author; numstat groups by file. Neither needs a plugin or a website.

steps.title: Count commits per author
steps.why: `shortlog -sn` is the fastest orientation there is: summary, numbered, sorted. Two people, six commits, and you already know who to ask about what.
steps.expect: Priya with four commits, Learner with two.

steps.title: See what each person actually wrote
steps.why: Without `-s`, shortlog groups the commit subjects under each author. This is the two-minute version of reading someone's entire contribution history.

steps.title: Find who owns a specific file
steps.why: Combine an author filter with a path. This is the honest way to pick a reviewer: not who is senior, but who has actually edited this file before.

verify.label: the owner of dosing.py is identifiable

steps.title: Which files churn the most
steps.why: `--numstat` prints added/removed line counts per file per commit. Feed it to sort and you have a churn report — the files that change constantly are usually where the bugs are.
commands: sh -c "git log --numstat --format='' | awk 'NF==3 {a[$3]+=$1+$2} END {for (f in a) print a[f], f}' | sort -rn"
steps.expect: dosing.py at the top: most edited, most risk.

steps.title: Activity over time
steps.why: `--date=short` with a format string gives you commits per day without leaving the terminal. Useful for 'when was this project actually being worked on'.

steps.title: Fix split identities with a mailmap
steps.why: Real repositories have the same person under three emails. `.mailmap` maps them to one canonical identity, and every git command that reports authors honours it — shortlog, blame and log included.
steps.expect: Priya now appears under her canonical name.

verify.label: the mailmap rewrote the displayed identity
verify.hint: write .mailmap mapping the canonical name to the commit email

verify.label: both contributors show in the summary
a mailmap is committed
verify.hint: write .mailmap and commit it — every git tool honours it

verify.label: file ownership is identifiable per path

pitfalls: Commit counts are a terrible performance metric and an excellent orientation tool. Use them to find people, never to rank them.
`git shortlog` with no revision reads from stdin when stdin is not a terminal -- in scripts and CI it silently prints nothing. Always pass HEAD.
shortlog reads authors, not committers. After a rebase the committer changes but the author does not — which is the correct behaviour.
`.mailmap` lives at the repository root and is honoured by log, blame and shortlog automatically. No config needed.
Path-scoped shortlog only sees commits that touched the path — a file created by a rename may look younger than it is.
cheatsheet: map several identities onto one person
